study.title: John 20 The Resurrection of Jesus, the Faith of the Disciples and the purpose of the Gospel
study.overview: John 20 presents a decisive sequence of testimonies about the resurrection of Jesus: the empty tomb, the encounter of Mary Magdalene with the Lord, the apparition to the disciples gathered in fear and then the confirmation given to Thomas. The chapter does not describe the exact moment in which Jesus rises; he gathers evidence and encounters that lead the disciples of confusion and mourning to confessed faith. The closing of the chapter explains the purpose of the Gospel: to bring to faith in Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God, so that readers may receive life in his name.

outline.title: The empty tomb and the initial faith of the beloved disciple
outline.explanation: Mary Magdalene finds the stone removed and runs to warn Peter and the other disciple. The tomb shows signs of order, not of hasty theft, and the beloved disciple sees and believes, although still without fully understanding Scripture about the necessity of the resurrection.

outline.title: Mary Magdalene meets Jesus and receives a mission
outline.explanation: While weeping, Mary remains next to the tomb, sees angels and then Jesus, but does not recognize him immediately. Recognition happens when Jesus calls it by name. Then she receives the command to announce to the brethren the ascension of Jesus to the Father.

outline.title: Jesus appears to the disciples and sends them
outline.explanation: In the evening of the first day of the week, Jesus comes to the midst of the disciples with the salutation of peace, shows the marks of the cross and fills them with joy. Then he sends them as the Father sent him and blows him over them, communicating the Holy Spirit and linking the church's mission to the forgiveness of sins.

outline.title: Thomas believes and the Gospel declares its purpose
outline.explanation: Thomas, absent from the first appearance, requires concrete evidence. Eight days later, Jesus confronts him in his doubt and leads him to the most direct confession of the chapter: Jesus is my Lord and my God. The chapter concludes by saying that the written signs aim to produce faith and life in the name of Jesus.

study.context: The text places events on the first day of the week, shortly after the crucifixion. There is mention of the tomb with rolling stone, a sign consistent with Jewish funeral customs mentioned by the commentators, but the chapter itself does not detail practices or dates beyond the narrative framework itself. The environment of the disciples is marked by fear, closed doors and uncertainty. John organizes the accounts in order to present successive witnesses of the resurrection, reinforcing the credibility of the apostolic testimony.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the resurrection of Jesus is the axis of the Christian faith: it confirms that Jesus is really the Christ and the Son of God, and not just a dead teacher. Faith is not born of mere imagination, but of encounter, witness and interpretation of the Scriptures. At the same time, the text shows that Jesus takes the initiative: he comes, calls by name, shows his wounds, restores the disciples and sends them. The peace he offers does not depend on the immediate disappearance of fear, but on the presence of the Risen One. The mission of the church is derived from the mission of Christ and depends on the action of the Holy Spirit. Thomas' confession acts as theological summit of the chapter, uniting recognition of the divine identity of Jesus and personal submission to him. The final purpose stated in 20.31 shows that the signs have pastoral and evangelistic purpose: to bring to faith and, through it, to life.

scholarViews.insight: Mary Magdalene naturally assumed that someone had taken the body, showing that her first reading of the empty tomb was confusing and human, not triumphalistic.
The evangelist closes with proofs of the resurrection, and Mary's presence with the tomb reveals her constant and fervent affection for Jesus.
Jesus sends the disciples for the same purpose of proclaiming the truth and leading sinners to God, sharing with them their mission.

questions: What, in your practice of faith, shows that you read the circumstances in the light of the resurrection of Jesus, and not just fear or loss?
Do you identify more with Mary, the beloved disciple or Thomas in this chapter? Why?
How can your church live the mission of Jesus more dependent on the Holy Spirit and more clearly about forgiveness?
study.practice: Read John 20 in prayer and identify a concrete movement of the chapter to imitate this week: to persevere as Mary, to witness as the disciples or to confess with Thomas. Then choose a person for whom you can simply announce that Jesus lives and calls by name. If there is fear, give this fear to the risen Christ and ask your peace to govern your words and attitudes.
study.uncertainty: There is a small textual variation mentioned in the notes in 20.31: some manuscripts bring the idea of continuing to believe, and others, of believing. The notes also note that the text does not describe the exact mode of the resurrection, but only its evidence and appearances. Other than that, the study was limited to the chapter and the scores provided, without resorting to external data.
